query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non‐equilibrium Mg-containing, lightweight high-entropy alloy, thermal activation triggers the diffusion and segregation of Mg from a homogenized solid solution to form discrete, stable Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates along phase or grain boundaries. These newly formed intermetallic phases then alter the local chemical environment, both modifying the nature of the protective high-temperature oxide scales that form and inducing localized galvanic cells that change the overall corrosion response.
generation.material_initial_state: A metastable, single-phase or mixed-phase high-entropy alloy (density <6 g/cm3) in which Mg is uniformly distributed within the lightweight matrix.
generation.intervention: Thermal aging (or high-temperature exposure) under oxidizing and corrosive environments.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures that activate atomic diffusion (e.g., several hundred °C) in air (or controlled oxidizing atmospheres) and in an electrolyte environment for corrosion testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and segregation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates at phase or grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Upon thermal exposure, Mg atoms diffuse out of the metastable, high-entropy matrix. Their segregation leads to the precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases that differ in chemical potential from the surrounding matrix. At high temperatures, these intermetallic regions promote the formation of modified oxide scales (by, for example, preferentially forming MgO or mixed oxides) that are more protective, while under corrosive conditions the electrochemical mismatch between the intermetallic phases and the matrix induces localized galvanic corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the initial homogenized state, aged samples will show a microstructure with clearly segregated Mg-rich intermetallics. This evolution will be accompanied by a change in high-temperature oxidation behavior (e.g., formation of a thinner or more adherent oxide scale) and altered corrosion performance (e.g., increased localized corrosion at intermetallic/matrix interfaces).
generation.baseline: The as-processed, non-equilibrium alloy displaying a homogeneous or nearly homogeneous Mg distribution with established hardness and compression properties, but without the evolved intermetallic segregation and its associated corrosion/oxidation features.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies when the alloy composition and processing favor metastability (i.e., where constituent-property differences drive intermetallic formation) and is contingent on exposure to thermal conditions sufficient to activate Mg diffusion; if the temperature is too low or the Mg content insufficient, the transformation may not occur.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative impact on oxidation and corrosion is expected, the precise balance—whether the new oxide scale is overall protective or if micron-scale galvanic cells accelerate localized corrosion—remains uncertain and likely depends on the volume fraction, size, and distribution of the precipitates.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same Mg-containing lightweight HEA. Subject one set to a high-temperature aging treatment (in air and a corrosive electrolyte) for a defined period and maintain the other set as an untreated control. Analyze microstructure evolution via transmission electron microscopy (TEM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect any segregation of Mg into intermetallic precipitates. Assess high-temperature oxidation behavior via mass gain measurements and oxide scale characterization, and perform potentiodynamic polarization tests to determine changes in corrosion rates.
measurements: Volume fraction and morphology of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates
Oxide scale thickness, composition, and adherence (via SEM/XRD)
Corrosion rate and potential differences (electrochemical tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, after thermal aging, no significant Mg segregation or Mg-rich intermetallic phase formation is detected and the oxidation and corrosion characteristics remain statistically indistinguishable from those of the control samples, the proposed mechanism is falsified.

The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. Abstract Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. Here, an unexpected ductile–brittle–ductile transition is discovered in a multiphase high‐entropy alloy (HEA) aged in an intermediate temperature regime. Unlike the classical thermal embrittlement driven by grain boundary effects, this transition originates from the dynamic evolution of local chemical order (LCO) and phase boundary (PB) configurations in HEAs. Aging within the embrittlement‐prone regime enhances chemical ordering, increases the density of ordered domains, and induces jagged PBs, collectively triggering plastic instability and the ductile−to−brittle transition. In contrast, aging outside this regime suppresses excessive ordering and promotes the formation of ductile interphase transition zones, facilitating a brittle−to−ductile recovery. The findings offer new insights into the thermal behavior of HEAs and challenge the established paradigm of thermal embrittlement. The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates.
